title: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
summary: Read compiled code the way compilers write it: ELF and Mach-O, System V and ARM64 calls, compiler idioms, C++, Rust and Go binaries, Ghidra scripting, firmware images, and patch diffing.
outcomes: Explain what ELF and Mach-O headers, segments, sections and symbol tables contain, and what survives stripping
Read x86-64 System V and ARM64 (AAPCS64 and Apple) code: arguments, returns, prologues and tail calls
Undo common compiler idioms such as division by multiplication, lookup and jump tables, and branchless selects
Recover structs, C++ vtables and RTTI, and recognise Rust and Go binaries from their runtime fingerprints
Automate Ghidra in headless mode with Java and Python scripts, and judge where decompiler output is wrong
Map, carve and audit a firmware image: headers, entropy, filesystem and boot-chain verification
Find the security fix between two stripped builds by matching functions, and report findings defensively

lessons.title: Beyond triage: what binary reverse engineering is for

blocks.md:
In the malware course you read PE files, x86-64 assembly and decompiler output to answer one question: what does this sample do? **Binary reverse engineering** (RE) in depth asks harder questions about any compiled program: how was it built, what was the source code likely to be, where is the bug, and what exactly did the vendor's patch change.

Tiny example: we wrote one short C file, `hello.c`, that sums the bytes of a string and prints the total. We compiled it three times. The same source became three different files, for two CPUs and two operating systems, and nothing in them says "hello.c" any more.

blocks.code:
$ aarch64-linux-musl-gcc -O2 -o hello_arm64 hello.c
$ x86_64-linux-musl-gcc  -O2 -o hello_x64   hello.c
$ clang -O2 -o hello_macho hello.c          # on an Apple Silicon Mac
$ file hello_arm64 hello_x64 hello_macho
hello_arm64: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, ARM aarch64, version 1 (SYSV), dynamically linked, interpreter /lib/ld-musl-aarch64.so.1, not stripped
hello_x64:   ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), dynamically linked, interpreter /lib/ld-musl-x86_64.so.1, not stripped
hello_macho: Mach-O 64-bit executable arm64
$ ls -l hello_*
-rwxr-xr-x  69984  hello_arm64
-rwxr-xr-x  33512  hello_macho
-rwxr-xr-x   7120  hello_x64
blocks.caption: Real output from the course lab (ls columns trimmed). Two cross-compilers built Linux programs on a Mac (musl is a small C standard library for Linux; each compiler is named after its CPU, OS and C library); clang built a native macOS one.

blocks.md:
Why go this deep? The jobs that need it:
- **Vulnerability research**: finding bugs in software whose source you do not have, such as router firmware or a closed-source driver.
- **Patch analysis**: a vendor ships a fix with a one-line advisory. Defenders compare the old and new binaries to learn what was really fixed and how urgent it is; attackers do the same, which is why the gap between patch and attack keeps shrinking.
- **Firmware and device audits**: routers, cameras and industrial controllers ship as binary images, often for ARM or MIPS (a RISC CPU family common in routers) CPUs rather than x86.
- **Malware written in newer languages**: Rust and Go malware compiles to code that looks nothing like C, and analysts need to recognise the compiler's fingerprints.

blocks.title: Compiling goes forward; reverse engineering walks back

scenes.caption: A compiler and linker turn source into a binary. Names, comments, types and structure are mostly thrown away on the way.
Reverse engineering starts from the binary. A disassembler decodes bytes into instructions; this needs only the CPU's instruction set.
A decompiler rebuilds C-like code from the instructions. It must guess what was lost: variable names, types, and which branches were loops.
You end with a model of the source, not the source itself. Every lesson in this course is about making that model accurate: knowing what each compiler does lets you undo it.

blocks.md: **Case: Ghidra goes public (2019).** On 5 March 2019, at the RSA Conference (a large annual security industry conference) in San Francisco, Rob Joyce, then the NSA's (US National Security Agency's) cybersecurity adviser, presented Ghidra and released it as open source, as [Wired reported](https://www.wired.com/story/nsa-ghidra-open-source-tool/). Joyce described it as a tool built for the agency's internal use; Wired counted 1.2 million lines of code, running on Windows, macOS and Linux, with support for several analysts working on one project. Ghidra had already been named in WikiLeaks' March 2017 "Vault 7" documents, but the code had never been seen. Wired noted that comparable tools such as IDA cost money, so this was the first time a tool of its calibre was free. This course uses Ghidra 12.2, run without its graphical interface.

**The lab and the rules.** Every binary in this course is one we compiled ourselves from harmless source code, so you can rebuild each one and check every output. The tools are free and need no system-wide installation:
- GNU **binutils** for each target CPU: `objdump` (disassembler), `readelf` (ELF structure), `nm` (symbols), `strings`, `strip`.
- macOS's `otool`, `nm` and `dyld_info` for Mach-O files.
- Ghidra run headless (from the command line) with small scripts.

We use only **static analysis**: reading files, never running them under a debugger. Debuggers such as GDB and WinDbg let you pause a running program and inspect its registers, which is the dynamic half of the craft and belongs in an isolated lab.

The legal line from security-basics still applies: analyse software you own or are authorised to test. Reverse engineering is also limited by licence terms and by laws on bypassing protection measures, such as section 1201 of the US Digital Millennium Copyright Act, which the [US Copyright Office](https://www.copyright.gov/1201/) administers with periodic exemptions. This course never touches copy protection, licence checks or downloaded vendor firmware.

blocks.question: Why does a binary built from `hello.c` no longer contain the word hello.c or the names of its local variables?
options: The compiler encrypts names to protect intellectual property
Names are stored, but only in the Mach-O version
The CPU executes only instructions and addresses, so the toolchain keeps names only where a later step (linker, loader, debugger) needs them
blocks.explain: Machine code refers to registers and addresses. Names survive only in tables that something else needs: the linker and loader need imported function names, and debuggers need debug info. Lesson 3 shows exactly which names survive stripping.

blocks.question: A vendor fixes a bug and publishes a one-line advisory. Why do both defenders and attackers compare the old and new binaries?
options: Because the binary diff shows what really changed, which tells defenders how urgent patching is and tells attackers where the bug was
To recover the vendor's source code exactly
Because advisories are legally required to be wrong
To check the file sizes match
blocks.explain: A diff of the two builds points at the changed function and the added check. That is how Rapid7 located the Juniper backdoor code two days after the advisory in 2015 (lesson 15), and why the time between a patch and attacks keeps shrinking.

lessons.title: ELF and Mach-O: the containers on Linux, devices and Macs

blocks.md:
The malware course taught **PE**, the Windows container. Linux, Android, most routers and many embedded devices use **ELF**, the Executable and Linkable Format; Apple's systems use **Mach-O**. All three answer the same questions for the operating system's loader: which CPU is this for, which bytes are code and which are data, where does execution start, and which libraries must be loaded first.

Tiny example: the first four bytes of every ELF file are `7f 45 4c 46`, which is the byte 0x7f followed by the letters E, L, F. Our Mach-O file starts with `cf fa ed fe`. Tools such as `file` decide what a file is from these **magic numbers**, not from its name.

blocks.code:
$ aarch64-linux-musl-readelf -h hello_arm64
ELF Header:
  Magic:   7f 45 4c 46 02 01 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
  Class:                             ELF64
  Data:                              2's complement, little endian
  Type:                              EXEC (Executable file)
  Machine:                           AArch64
  Entry point address:               0x400628
  Start of program headers:          64 (bytes into file)
  Start of section headers:          68320 (bytes into file)
  Number of program headers:         8
  Number of section headers:         26
blocks.caption: readelf output, trimmed to the fields discussed. Byte 4 (02) means 64-bit, byte 5 (01) little-endian.

blocks.title: The first 20 bytes of two ELF files and one Mach-O

scenes.caption: Bytes 0 to 3 are the ELF magic in both ELF files: 0x7f then the ASCII codes for E, L and F.
Byte 4 is the class: 02 is 64-bit (our ARM64 hello), 01 is 32-bit (a MIPS build of a toy web server). Byte 5 is the byte order: 01 little-endian, 02 big-endian.
Bytes 18 and 19 hold e_machine, the CPU type, in the file's own byte order: b7 00 is 0xb7 (AArch64) read little-endian; 00 08 is 8 (MIPS) read big-endian.
Mach-O starts differently: cf fa ed fe is MH_MAGIC_64 (0xfeedfacf) stored little-endian, then the CPU type 0x0100000c, which otool prints as ARM64.

blocks.md:
An ELF file has two views of the same bytes:
- **Program headers** describe **segments**: the ranges the kernel and dynamic loader map into memory, with permissions. Our file has two `LOAD` segments: one readable and executable (R E) holding code and constants, one readable and writable (RW) holding data. This view is all a program needs to run.
- **Section headers** describe **sections**: finer, named pieces that the linker and analysis tools use, such as `.text` (code), `.rodata` (read-only data like strings), `.data` and `.bss` (writable data, `.bss` zero-filled), and `.symtab` (symbol names).

Because the loader uses only segments, a binary can run with its section headers removed or corrupted. Tools that rely on sections, such as objdump, then see little or nothing, while tools that read the program headers (readelf -l, Ghidra) can still follow the segments.

blocks.code:
$ aarch64-linux-musl-readelf -lW hello_arm64      (trimmed)
  Type    Offset   VirtAddr           FileSiz  MemSiz   Flg Align
  INTERP  0x000200 0x0000000000400200 0x00001a 0x00001a R   0x1
      [Requesting program interpreter: /lib/ld-musl-aarch64.so.1]
  LOAD    0x000000 0x0000000000400000 0x0008e4 0x0008e4 R E 0x10000
  LOAD    0x00fdf0 0x000000000041fdf0 0x000240 0x000278 RW  0x10000
  GNU_RELRO 0x00fdf0 0x000000000041fdf0 0x000210 0x000210 R 0x1

 Section to Segment mapping:
   02     .interp .hash .gnu.hash .dynsym .dynstr .rela.dyn .rela.plt .init .plt .text .fini .rodata .eh_frame_hdr .eh_frame
   03     .init_array .fini_array .dynamic .got .got.plt .data .bss
blocks.caption: The first LOAD segment holds code (.text) and constants (.rodata); the second holds writable data. MemSiz is larger than FileSiz in the second because .bss takes no space in the file.

blocks.md:
**Dynamic linking.** `printf` is not inside our binary; it lives in the C library. The `INTERP` segment names the **dynamic loader** (`/lib/ld-musl-aarch64.so.1`), which runs first, loads the libraries and fills in addresses. Two tables make this work:
- The **GOT** (global offset table): a table of addresses in writable memory that the loader fills with the real locations of imported functions and variables.
- The **PLT** (procedure linkage table): tiny stubs in the code. A call to `printf` really calls `printf@plt`, which jumps through the GOT entry. In disassembly you will see `bl 400550 <printf@plt>`.

The names to resolve sit in `.dynsym` and `.dynstr`, the dynamic symbol table. Some systems also support **IFUNC** (indirect function) symbols: a resolver function runs at load time and picks which version of a function to use, for example one optimised for the current CPU.

**Case: the XZ Utils backdoor (2024).** On 29 March 2024 Andres Freund, investigating odd symptoms on Debian unstable (sid) (SSH logins using a lot of CPU, and errors from the memory checker Valgrind), reported on the oss-security mailing list (not linked: it attaches the backdoor's object file) that the upstream xz repository and the release tarballs of xz 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 were backdoored ([CVE-2024-3094](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2024/03/29/reported-supply-chain-compromise-affecting-xz-utils-data-compression-library-cve-2024-3094)). [LWN's analysis](https://lwn.net/Articles/967192/) shows how the attack lived inside the dynamic linking machinery just described. A precompiled object file hidden in test data was linked into liblzma. Its fake IFUNC resolvers for `crc32` and `crc64` ran while the loader was still working, registered an audit hook (a callback the dynamic linker makes while resolving symbols), and waited for OpenSSH's `RSA_public_decrypt` to be resolved so it could substitute its own code. Some distributions linked sshd to libsystemd, which pulls in liblzma.

The same case shows why reverse engineers needed the binary, not just the source: the backdoor was 87 KB of compiled code that never existed as source code (it sat in the repository only in encoded form, inside binary test files), and LWN notes it hid its strings (such as `RSA_public_decrypt@got.plt`) in a trie, a compact lookup structure, so a plain `strings` run would not show them. Analysts recovered its behaviour by disassembling and decompiling that object file.

**Defender view.** Detection came from behaviour: CPU time and Valgrind errors that did not fit. Prevention lessons include building from the reviewed repository rather than a release tarball, reproducible builds that can be compared byte for byte, and watching which libraries security-critical daemons such as sshd load.

**Mach-O in one paragraph.** A Mach-O file is a header followed by **load commands**, each telling the loader one thing. `otool -l hello_macho` lists 17 of them, including `LC_SEGMENT_64` for the segments `__PAGEZERO`, `__TEXT` (code in section `__text`, C strings in `__cstring`, call stubs in `__stubs`), `__DATA_CONST` (with the `__got`) and `__LINKEDIT` (linker data), plus `LC_MAIN` (entry point), `LC_LOAD_DYLIB` (a library to load), `LC_FUNCTION_STARTS` and `LC_CODE_SIGNATURE`. A **universal** (fat) file packs several Mach-O files for different CPUs into one; `lipo` lists and extracts them.

blocks.question: A Linux router binary has its section headers zeroed out. Will it still run, and why?
options: No: the loader needs .text to find the code
Only if it is statically linked
Yes: the kernel and dynamic loader map the file using program headers (segments); sections are for linkers and tools
blocks.explain: Loading uses the segment view. Removing section headers hurts tools that rely on them, such as objdump, but execution is unaffected.

blocks.question: In the readelf output, why does the second LOAD segment have MemSiz 0x278 but FileSiz 0x240?
options: The extra 0x38 bytes are .bss, zero-initialised data that is created in memory but stored as nothing in the file
blocks.explain: `.bss` holds zero-initialised globals; storing zeros would waste space, so the loader allocates and zeroes them. The section table shows .bss with size 0x38, exactly the difference.

blocks.prompt: Byte 5 of our MIPS build is 02 (big-endian). Its e_machine field holds the value 8. Predict the two bytes at offsets 18 and 19.
blocks.reveal: `00 08`. In a big-endian file the most significant byte comes first, so the 16-bit value 8 is stored as 00 then 08. In the little-endian ARM64 file, 0xb7 is stored as `b7 00`. Reading multi-byte fields in the wrong byte order is one of the most common beginner mistakes with MIPS and older ARM firmware.

lessons.title: Symbols, stripping and debug info: what survives

blocks.md:
A **symbol** is a name attached to an address: a function, a global variable, an imported routine. Compilers write symbols so that the linker can connect pieces, and so that debuggers and crash reports can say "crashed in checksum" rather than "crashed at 0x400790". **Stripping** removes the symbols a program does not need to run. Release builds are usually stripped, so the first job on an unknown binary is to know what stripping removes and what it cannot remove.

Tiny example: `nm hello_arm64` lists `checksum` at 0x400780 and `main` at 0x4005a0. After `strip`, `nm` says "no symbols", yet `printf` and `strlen` are still named. Why those two? Because the dynamic loader needs them.

blocks.code:
$ aarch64-linux-musl-nm hello_arm64 | grep -E "checksum|main|printf|strlen"
                 U __libc_start_main
0000000000400780 T checksum
00000000004005a0 T main
                 U printf
                 U strlen
$ aarch64-linux-musl-strip -o hello_arm64_stripped hello_arm64
$ aarch64-linux-musl-nm hello_arm64_stripped
aarch64-linux-musl-nm: hello_arm64_stripped: no symbols
$ aarch64-linux-musl-nm -D hello_arm64_stripped | grep " U "
                 U __libc_start_main
                 U printf
                 U strlen
blocks.caption: T means a function defined in the file's code; U means undefined here and imported. -D reads the dynamic symbol table, which stripping must keep.

blocks.md:
There are two symbol tables in a dynamically linked ELF file:
- `.symtab` (the full table, in a section the loader never maps). `strip` deletes it.
- `.dynsym` (dynamic symbols, inside a loaded segment). It must stay, because the loader uses it to find imports and exports. So imports such as `printf` are always visible, which is why reading imports works even on stripped binaries, as you did with PE import tables.

A **statically linked** binary copies the library code inside. Then even `printf` is just another unnamed function. With symbols, Ghidra found 76 functions in our static build (its symbol table names 75 distinct function addresses); after stripping, Ghidra's analysis found 65 functions and could name only one of them (`entry`, the start address from the ELF header).

blocks.title: Functions Ghidra finds and names in our static build

scenes.caption: With symbols: Ghidra finds 76 functions (main, checksum and the C library code copied in) and names 75 of them from the symbol table.
The same file stripped: Ghidra finds 65 functions by following calls from the entry point, but only one keeps a name (entry); 64 get placeholders like FUN_00400680.
And 11 functions are not found at all: code that nothing reaches by a direct call or jump is easy to miss once its symbol is gone.

blocks.md:
That last point matters. In our dynamic build GCC **inlined** `checksum` into `main` (copied its body into the caller) but also kept a separate copy at 0x400780 because the function was not `static`. Nothing calls that copy. With symbols, Ghidra knows it is a function. After stripping, Ghidra's list of functions in the stripped file had no entry at 0x400780 at all: its bytes are still there, but analysis that starts from the entry point and follows calls never reaches them.

**Library identification** recovers names in stripped static binaries by matching known code. IDA's **FLIRT** ([Fast Library Identification and Recognition Technology](https://docs.hex-rays.com/user-guide/signatures/flirt)) recognises standard library functions from byte signatures; Ghidra's [Function ID](https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/ghidra/tree/master/Ghidra/Features/FunctionID) does the same with hashes of function bodies. Both only work when a signature database exists for that compiler and library version.

**Debug information** is far richer than symbols. Compiled with `-g`, our binary gained eight `.debug_*` sections in the **DWARF** format, the standard debug format for ELF (the name is a pun on ELF; its creator Brian Russell expanded it as Debugging With Attributed Record Formats, per the [DWARF FAQ](https://dwarfstd.org/faq.html)): types, variable names, and a **line table** mapping each address to a source line. Its decoded form says address 0x400780 is `hello.c` line 6, the first line of `checksum`. Debug info is almost never shipped, but leaks happen: a build with `-g` uploaded by mistake makes reverse engineering nearly trivial.

**Mach-O keeps a hint.** Stripping our Mac binary left `nm` showing only the imports and the linker's `__mh_execute_header`, but the `LC_FUNCTION_STARTS` load command survives, and `dyld_info -function_starts` still lists both function addresses (0x100000460 and 0x100000560). The table exists to help tools such as crash reporters find function boundaries; it helps reverse engineers too.

blocks.code:
$ aarch64-linux-musl-gcc -O2 -g -o hello_dbg hello.c
$ aarch64-linux-musl-objdump --dwarf=decodedline hello_dbg   (first lines)
File name                        Line number    Starting address
hello.c                                    6            0x400780
hello.c                                    7            0x400780
hello.c                                    8            0x400780
hello.c                                    7            0x40078c
hello.c                                    9            0x4007a0
$ strip hello_macho_stripped && dyld_info -function_starts hello_macho_stripped
hello_macho_stripped [arm64]:
    -function_starts:
        0x100000460  __TEXT,__text
        0x100000560  __TEXT,__text+256
blocks.caption: Real output (repeated rows and some columns trimmed). Several lines map to one address because optimised code mixes statements.

blocks.md: **Defender view.** Strip release builds, but keep the exact debug files privately, indexed by a **build ID** (a hash the linker stores in a note section; our Go binary's `file` output shows one). Crash reports from the field can then be symbolised on your side. Linux distributions publish debug files through servers such as [debuginfod](https://sourceware.org/elfutils/Debuginfod.html), so analysts of open-source binaries can fetch symbols that match a build ID. Stripping is not a security control: it slows a reverse engineer down, it does not stop one.

blocks.question: A stripped, dynamically linked ELF binary calls `connect` and `SSL_write`. Will those names appear in `nm -D` output?
options: Yes, imported functions stay in .dynsym because the dynamic loader must resolve them at run time
Only if the binary was built with -g
blocks.explain: The dynamic symbol table is part of what the program needs to run, so strip cannot delete it. Imports are a reliable map of behaviour even in stripped binaries.

blocks.question: After stripping, a function that exists in the file never appears in Ghidra's function list. What is the most likely reason?
options: Nothing calls it, so analysis that follows calls and jumps from the entry point never reaches it
blocks.explain: Strip removes names, not code. Without a symbol, a function is found only if something references it. Look for gaps of unexplained code between known functions and define functions there by hand.

lessons.title: x86-64 on Linux and macOS: the System V calling convention

blocks.md:
The malware course used the Microsoft x64 calling convention (arguments in `rcx`, `rdx`, `r8`, `r9`, plus a 32-byte shadow store). Linux, BSD and macOS on x86-64 follow a different contract, the [System V AMD64 ABI](https://gitlab.com/x86-psABIs/x86-64-ABI) (named after UNIX System V, whose generic ABI it extends). Reading Linux binaries means switching contracts.

Tiny example: `sum8(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8)` adds eight numbers. Before the call you will see 1 to 6 loaded into six registers and 7 and 8 pushed onto the stack. Knowing the contract, you can recover the call's arguments without any source.

The integer rules, from the ABI document:
- Arguments 1 to 6 go in `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `rcx`, `r8`, `r9`. Further arguments go on the stack, the 7th at the lowest address.
- The result comes back in `rax` (and `rdx` for a second 8-byte part).
- **Callee-saved** registers (a function must restore them before returning): `rbx`, `rbp`, `r12` to `r15`. All others may be overwritten by any call, so the caller must save what it needs.
- The stack must be 16-byte aligned just before a `call`.
- The **red zone**: 128 bytes below `rsp` that signal and interrupt handlers must not touch, so a **leaf function** (one that calls nothing) can keep its locals there without moving `rsp`.
- For a call to a variadic function such as `printf`, `al` holds an upper bound on the number of vector registers used for arguments.

blocks.caption: abi.c, compiled with x86_64-linux-musl-gcc -O2 -fno-inline (GCC 14.2) so each function stays separate.

blocks.code:
0000000000000000 <sum8>:
   0:  add    rdi,rsi
   3:  add    rdi,rdx
   6:  add    rdi,rcx
   9:  add    rdi,r8
   c:  lea    rax,[rdi+r9*1]
  10:  add    rax,QWORD PTR [rsp+0x8]
  15:  add    rax,QWORD PTR [rsp+0x10]
  1a:  ret
0000000000000020 <make_point>:
  20:  mov    QWORD PTR [rdi],rsi
  23:  mov    rax,rdi
  26:  mov    QWORD PTR [rdi+0x8],rdx
  2a:  mov    QWORD PTR [rdi+0x10],rcx
  2e:  ret
0000000000000030 <caller>:
  30:  push   0x8
  32:  mov    r9d,0x6
  38:  mov    r8d,0x5
  3e:  mov    ecx,0x4
  43:  push   0x7
  45:  mov    edx,0x3
  4a:  mov    esi,0x2
  4f:  mov    edi,0x1
  54:  call   59 <caller+0x29>
            55: R_X86_64_PLT32  sum8-0x4
  59:  pop    rdx
  5a:  pop    rcx
  5b:  ret
blocks.caption: objdump -dr -M intel output (padding nops between functions omitted). The call target is not filled in yet: this is an unlinked object file, and the relocation line tells the linker to patch in sum8.

blocks.title: The stack when sum8 starts (8-byte slots, lowest address on the left)

scenes.caption: caller pushes 8 first, then 7, so 7 ends up at the lower address: the 7th argument always sits closest to the return address.
call pushes the return address. At sum8's first instruction rsp points at it, so the 7th argument is at rsp+0x8 and the 8th at rsp+0x10, exactly the two memory operands in sum8.
sum8 is a leaf function and needs no locals, so it never moves rsp. After ret, caller's two pops (into rdx and rcx, values ignored) are just a compact way to drop the 16 bytes it pushed.

blocks.md:
`make_point` shows the rule for a large return value. A 24-byte struct does not fit in `rax` and `rdx`, so the ABI classifies it as MEMORY: the caller reserves space and passes its address as a **hidden first argument** in `rdi`. Every real argument shifts by one register: `x` arrives in `rsi`, `y` in `rdx`, `z` in `rcx`, and the function returns the hidden pointer in `rax`.

This trips up decompilers and people alike. If you see a function that writes through `rdi` and returns `rdi`, suspect a struct return, and expect the source to have one fewer parameter than the registers suggest.

Do not apply Windows habits to Linux binaries. On Windows the first argument is in `rcx`; on Linux and macOS `rcx` is the fourth. Misreading the convention shifts every argument by several positions and makes a correct analysis look nonsensical. Check the file format first: PE means Microsoft x64, ELF or Mach-O on x86-64 means System V.

blocks.question: In a Linux x86-64 binary, a function is called after `mov rdi, rbx; mov esi, 0x100; mov rdx, r12`. What are its first three arguments?
options: rbx, 0x100 and r12, in that order
Only 0x100; rdi is the return address
blocks.explain: System V passes arguments 1, 2 and 3 in rdi, rsi and rdx. esi is the low half of rsi; writing it zero-extends into rsi.

blocks.question: A function begins `mov QWORD PTR [rdi], rsi` and ends `mov rax, rdi; ret`. Its source most likely
options: returns a large struct by value, with rdi as the hidden pointer to the caller's space
blocks.explain: Writing through rdi and returning rdi is the MEMORY-class return pattern: the caller passed the destination address as a hidden first argument.

blocks.prompt: A leaf function stores a local at `[rsp-0x10]` and never subtracts from rsp. Is that a bug?
blocks.reveal: No. It is using the red zone: the 128 bytes below rsp that the System V ABI reserves, so signal and interrupt handlers will not overwrite them. Only leaf functions can rely on it, because a call would push a return address into that area. The Windows x64 convention has no red zone.

lessons.title: ARM64 from zero: registers, loads, stores and branches

blocks.md:
Apple Silicon Macs (including the one that built this course's lab), most phones and many embedded devices run **ARM64**, also called **AArch64** (Arm's name for the 64-bit execution state of its architecture). The prereq course showed one ARM64 snippet; here you learn to read it properly.

Tiny example: `ldrb w3, [x0], #1` reads one byte from the address in `x0` into register `w3`, then adds 1 to `x0`. One instruction does what a C loop writes as `c = *p++`. ARM64 packs a lot into each instruction, but every instruction is exactly 4 bytes long (the addresses in any listing step by 4), which makes disassembly reliable: there is no ambiguity about where an instruction starts.

**Registers.** There are 31 general registers, `x0` to `x30`, each 64 bits. Writing `w0` uses the low 32 bits of `x0` (and clears the top half). Special names:
- `sp`: the stack pointer. `xzr` / `wzr`: reads as zero, writes are discarded.
- `x29`: the **frame pointer** (FP). `x30`: the **link register** (LR), which `bl` (branch with link) fills with the return address instead of pushing it on the stack.
- The program counter is not a general register; you see it only through branches and PC-relative addressing.

**Load/store architecture.** Arithmetic works only on registers. Memory is touched only by loads (`ldr`, `ldrb` byte, `ldrh` 16-bit, `ldp` pair) and stores (`str`, `strb`, `strh`, `stp`). Compare with x86, where `add rax, QWORD PTR [rsp+0x8]` reads memory inside an add.

The calling convention is Arm's [AAPCS64](https://github.com/ARM-software/abi-aa/blob/main/aapcs64/aapcs64.rst) (Procedure Call Standard for the Arm 64-bit Architecture):
- `x0` to `x7`: arguments and results. `x8`: the **indirect result location**, the address where a large returned struct should go (the job `rdi` did as a hidden argument on x86-64).
- `x9` to `x15`: scratch, may be clobbered by calls. `x16` and `x17` (IP0, IP1): scratch that the linker may use in PLT stubs and veneers (small trampolines for far calls).
- `x18`: the **platform register**, reserved on some systems.
- `x19` to `x28`: callee-saved. A function that uses them must save and restore them.

Our `abi.c` from the last lesson, compiled for ARM64, passes all eight `sum8` arguments in `x0` to `x7`, returns the struct through `x8` (`stp x0, x1, [x8]` then `str x2, [x8, #16]`), and `caller` ends with `b 0 <sum8>`: a plain branch, not a call, because the result of `sum8` is returned unchanged. That is a **tail call**: sum8 will return straight to caller's caller.
